human beings. Man who subjugates the threatening world
more and more to his own purposes, seeks also to integrate
into the structure of his ordered world that mystery which
once peered at him with a thousand eyes out of the surround-
ing darkness and lurked around his footsteps. He seeks to
give it a place which, though still imparting awe and fear,
shines with the clear light of daily life and becomes the centre
of a regularized cult. In fact, in proportion as man devotes
himself with efficiency and enthusiasm to such ordered
worship, his primal fear is benumbed and the mystery of his
existence concealed by his religion.
This is illustrated by the story of the very place on which
Paul delivered his discourse, for it was the shrine at which
those dread demons of blood vengeance, the Erinnyes, were
worshipped. Yet their cult resulted in their being given the
name of the Eumenides, the gracious ones.
This then is the superstitious aspect of heathen religion; it
breathes, not the true fear of the living God, but deep-rooted
anxiety in face of the strange mystery of the world, and such
religion spells also the attempt to master this anxiety
through a human effort to secure control of the mystery and
to integrate it with the norm of human life. Thus man tries
to calm his anxious mind and to attain a secure mastery of
his existence.
II
In all this, have we been speaking of a remote past, which
may be of interest to us but which fundamentally no longer
concerns us? Or have we been speaking essentially of ourselves
also? Have modern men ceased to feel that anxiety? Is the
world and human existence no longer a dark mystery for
them? Have they ceased to practise the art of trying to
control the mystery? Of trying to control it precisely through
the means of religion?
